items.title: Evolution of Planning & the Planning Commission
items.body:
**In one line:** India chose to steer its economy through government planning, and from 1950 the Planning Commission drew up Five-Year Plans and decided how central money was shared out.

**Why it is asked:** The pre-independence plans, the Commission's non-statutory status and the National Development Council's role are classic one-mark facts.

## Pre-independence roots

Organised planning ideas predate 1947:

| Plan | Year | Proposer |
|---|---|---|
| Visvesvaraya Plan | 1934 | M. Visvesvaraya (*Planned Economy for India*) |
| National Planning Committee | 1938 | Set up by Subhash Chandra Bose (Congress president); chaired by Nehru |
| Bombay Plan | 1944 | J.R.D. Tata, G.D. Birla & industrialists |
| Gandhian Plan | 1944 | S.N. Agarwal |
| People's Plan | 1945 | M.N. Roy |

Early thinkers Dadabhai Naoroji and M. Visvesvaraya shaped the idea of an organised, self-sustaining economy.

## The Planning Commission (1950)

- Set up by an **executive resolution of the Government of India in 1950** — a **non-statutory, non-constitutional** body.
- **Prime Minister** was ex-officio **Chairperson**; a full-time Deputy Chairman ran it.
- Task: frame **Five-Year Plans**, set national priorities, **allocate central funds** to states/sectors, and monitor progress.
- Followed a **centralised, top-down, socialist-influenced** model (Soviet inspiration) with the **public sector** as the main growth driver.

## Objectives & approaches

- Core objectives: **growth, equity/social justice, modernisation, self-reliance**.
- Post-1991 shift from **centralised to indicative planning** (state as facilitator).
- **73rd & 74th Amendments** enabled **decentralised planning** through PRIs and urban local bodies.

## National Development Council (NDC)

- Set up in **1952** by executive resolution (non-statutory); chaired by the **Prime Minister**, with all **Chief Ministers, Union Cabinet Ministers and Planning Commission members**.
- It was the **apex body that reviewed and approved every Five-Year Plan** before implementation. Along with **Parliament**, the NDC is the body most closely associated with 'planning' in India — the **Finance Commission and line ministries (Rural/Urban Development) are NOT**.

### In short

**The story in brief.** The background, the cause-and-effect and every term used are explained in the sections above; the essential facts to carry into the exam are these.

**TL;DR**

- Planning Commission was set up in 1950 by an executive resolution — non-statutory and non-constitutional, chaired by the PM.
- National Development Council (NDC, 1952): PM-chaired, includes all CMs; the apex body that approved the Five-Year Plans. NDC and Parliament are associated with planning, not the Finance Commission.
- Pre-independence plans: Visvesvaraya Plan (1934), NPC (1938, Bose/Nehru), Bombay Plan (1944, Tata & Birla), People's Plan (1945, M.N. Roy).
- Four objectives of Indian planning: growth, equity, modernisation and self-reliance.
- India shifted from centralised planning to indicative planning after the 1991 reforms.
- 73rd and 74th Constitutional Amendments promoted decentralised planning via local bodies.

items.title: The Five-Year Plans (1951-2017) at a glance
items.body:
**In one line:** Between 1951 and 2017 India ran twelve Five-Year Plans, each with its own economic model and theme, moving from farming-first to heavy industry to inclusive growth.

**Why it is asked:** Which plan used which model, which plan failed, and which was the last are repeatedly tested.

## Models & milestones

| Plan | Period | Model / Theme | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| First | 1951-56 | Harrod-Domar; agriculture, irrigation | Bhakra-Nangal & Hirakud dams, IIT Kharagpur; **target exceeded** (3.6% vs 2.1%) |
| Second | 1956-61 | Mahalanobis; heavy industry | Establishment of steel plants at Bhilai/Rourkela/Durgapur; PSU-led |
| Third | 1961-66 | Gadgil-Yojana; self-reliance | **Failed** (wars 1962/65, drought) → Plan Holiday |
| Plan Holiday | 1966-69 | Annual plans | Food security; sowed the Green Revolution |
| Fourth | 1969-74 | Green Revolution, self-reliance | HYV seeds; hit by poor monsoons & 1971 war |
| Fifth | 1974-78 | 'Garibi Hatao' | Minimum Needs Programme; cut short in 1978 |
| Rolling Plan | 1978-80 | Flexible annual revision | Janata government; later abandoned |
| Sixth | 1980-85 | Poverty, employment, infra | Family planning; met target |
| Seventh | 1985-90 | Productivity, employment | 6.0% growth; IT sector begins |
| Annual Plans | 1990-92 | Crisis stabilisation | **1991 LPG reforms** launched |
| Eighth | 1992-97 | LPG era, private sector | 6.8% growth (highest so far) |
| Ninth | 1997-2002 | Growth with social justice | 5.4% vs 6.5% target |
| Tenth | 2002-07 | 8% growth target | 7.3–7.6% achieved (sources differ) |
| Eleventh | 2007-12 | Faster & inclusive growth | Global financial crisis |
| Twelfth | 2012-17 | 'Faster, Sustainable and More Inclusive Growth' | **Last Five-Year Plan** |

## Growth models to remember

- **Harrod-Domar** (First): growth driven by saving & investment rate.
- **Mahalanobis** (Second): heavy capital-goods industries for long-run growth.
- **Gadgil-Yojana** (Third): decentralised balanced regional development.

### In short

**The story in brief.** The background, the cause-and-effect and every term used are explained in the sections above; the essential facts to carry into the exam are these.

**TL;DR**

- First Plan (1951-56): Harrod-Domar model, agriculture focus, exceeded target at 3.6%.
- Second Plan (1956-61): Mahalanobis model, heavy industry, set up Bhilai/Rourkela/Durgapur steel plants.
- Third Plan (1961-66): Gadgil-Yojana; failed due to Indo-China (1962) and Indo-Pak (1965) wars and drought.
- Plan Holiday (1966-69): three annual plans replaced the regular plan.
- Fifth Plan (1974-78) used the 'Garibi Hatao' slogan and Minimum Needs Programme.
- Eighth Plan (1992-97) coincided with LPG reforms; Twelfth Plan (2012-17) was the last Five-Year Plan.
- Twelfth Plan (2012-17) objective slogan: 'Faster, Sustainable and More Inclusive Growth'; Eleventh Plan: 'faster and more inclusive growth'.

items.title: NITI Aayog — structure, role & federalism
items.body:
**In one line:** In 2015 the Planning Commission was replaced by NITI Aayog, a policy think-tank that advises the government and the states rather than allocating funds to them.

**Why it is asked:** The Planning-Commission-versus-NITI contrast, NITI's current office-holders and its flagship indices are frequent, current-affairs-linked questions.

## From Commission to NITI Aayog

The Planning Commission was dissolved and **NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India)** was created on **1 January 2015** by a **Union Cabinet resolution**, because the old top-down model no longer fit the **post-1991 liberalised, market-driven economy** (rigidity, over-centralisation, weak state consultation, limited private-sector role).

## Structure

- **Chairperson:** Prime Minister.
- **Governing Council:** includes the Chief Ministers of all states + UT Lt. Governors/administrators.
- **Vice-Chairman:** nominated by the PM (2026: **Ashok Lahiri**).
- **CEO:** senior civil servant who heads it on a day-to-day basis — the Chief Executive Officer (2026: **Anurag Jain**); plus full-time & part-time members and ex-officio members.

## Role vs the Planning Commission

| Aspect | Planning Commission | NITI Aayog |
|---|---|---|
| Nature | Fund-allocating planning body | Policy **think-tank / advisor** |
| Approach | Top-down, centralised | Bottom-up, **cooperative federalism** |
| Funds | Allocated funds to states | **No fund-allocation** role (now with **Finance Commission**) |
| Method | Five-Year Plans | 3-Year Action Agenda, 7-Year Strategy, 15-Year Vision |

## Key initiatives

- **Aspirational Districts Programme**, **SDG India Index**, **National Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI)**, **Atal Innovation Mission** (Atal Tinkering Labs), **India Innovation Index**, **Composite Water Management Index**.
- Promotes **cooperative & competitive federalism** and data-driven, real-time monitoring.

## Viksit Bharat @2047

- NITI Aayog anchors the **Viksit Bharat @2047** vision — making India a **developed nation by 2047** (centenary of independence), covering economic growth, social progress, environmental sustainability and good governance.

### In short

**The story in brief.** The background, the cause-and-effect and every term used are explained in the sections above; the essential facts to carry into the exam are these.

**TL;DR**

- NITI Aayog was established on 1 January 2015 by a Cabinet resolution as a policy think-tank; the PM is its Chairperson.
- Governing Council comprises all state Chief Ministers; a Vice-Chairman and a CEO run it (2026: Ashok Lahiri and Anurag Jain).
- Unlike the Planning Commission, NITI Aayog has no power to allocate funds — devolution now rests with the Finance Commission.
- Bodies NOT part of NITI Aayog: the Finance Commission (constitutional, Art 280; it handles the devolution of central taxes to States) and the FSDC (chaired by the Finance Minister, financial stability).
- NITI Aayog replaced Five-Year Plans with a 3-Year Action Agenda, 7-Year Strategy and 15-Year Vision.
- Flagship initiatives: Aspirational Districts Programme, SDG India Index, National MPI, Atal Innovation Mission.
- Viksit Bharat @2047 is the vision to make India a developed nation by 2047, anchored by NITI Aayog.

items.title: Before 1950 — Every Pre-Independence Plan and Its Author
items.body:
**In one line:** long before the Planning Commission, Congress, engineers, industrialists, Gandhians and radicals each drew up a plan — and examiners pair each plan with its year and author.

**Why it is asked:** "Match the plan with its proposer" is the commonest planning-history question in state PSC papers.

## The full list

**The story**

| Plan / body | Year | Author | One-line idea |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Agricultural Development Plan** | **1928** | Indian National Congress | Land reforms, cooperative farming, irrigation |
| **Visvesvaraya Plan** | **1934** | **M. Visvesvaraya** (book *Planned Economy for India*) | **10-year** plan of rapid **industrialisation** to double national income |
| **FICCI Plan** | 1930s | Federation of Indian Chambers of Commerce and Industry | Private-sector-led growth with tariff protection |
| **National Planning Committee** | **1938** | Set up by **Subhash Chandra Bose** (Congress president), chaired by **Jawaharlal Nehru** | Mixed economy, self-sufficiency, science and technology |
| **Bombay Plan** | **1944** | **J.R.D. Tata, G.D. Birla** and other industrialists | **15-year** plan; state investment in basic industries (steel, power, railways) |
| **Gandhian Plan** | **1944** | **S.N. Agarwal** (Shriman Narayan) | **Gram Swaraj**, cottage and small industries, decentralisation |
| **People's Plan** | **1945** | **M.N. Roy** | Socialist plan — nationalisation of industry and banks, collective farming |
| **Sarvodaya Plan** | **1950** | **Jayaprakash Narayan** | Gandhian-Sarvodaya ideas; land reforms, village self-sufficiency |

- Early thinkers **Dadabhai Naoroji** and **M. Visvesvaraya** shaped the idea of a planned, self-sustaining economy.
- India's planning was **influenced by the Soviet model** of centralised control and heavy industry.

## Don't confuse

- **Bombay Plan** = industrialists, **15** years; **Visvesvaraya Plan** = engineer, **10** years.
- **Gandhian Plan** (S.N. Agarwal, 1944) ≠ **Sarvodaya Plan** (J.P. Narayan, 1950); **People's Plan** = **M.N. Roy**.

**TL;DR**
- 1928 Congress agricultural plan; 1934 Visvesvaraya (10-year, industrialisation); 1938 NPC (Bose/Nehru).
- 1944 Bombay Plan (Tata, Birla; 15-year); 1944 Gandhian Plan (S.N. Agarwal); 1945 People's Plan (M.N. Roy); 1950 Sarvodaya Plan (J.P. Narayan).
keyPoints: Agricultural Development Plan (1928) — Indian National Congress.
Visvesvaraya Plan (1934) — M. Visvesvaraya's 10-year plan in 'Planned Economy for India'.
Bombay Plan (1944) — J.R.D. Tata, G.D. Birla and others; a 15-year plan.
Gandhian Plan (1944) — S.N. Agarwal; People's Plan (1945) — M.N. Roy; Sarvodaya Plan (1950) — Jayaprakash Narayan.
National Planning Committee (1938) — set up by Subhash Chandra Bose, chaired by Nehru.
Indian planning was influenced by the Soviet model of centralised planning.

items.title: Five-Year Plans — Targets, Firsts and Signature Facts
items.body:
**In one line:** each Plan has one or two signature facts — a model, a slogan, a project or a target — and these are what examiners ask.

**Why it is asked:** UPSC 2019 and 2014 asked plan-specific features; state PSCs ask "which plan…" one-liners.

## Plan-by-plan signature facts

**The story**

| Plan | Signature facts |
|---|---|
| **First (1951-56)** | **Harrod-Domar** model; agriculture got about **44.6%** of outlay; target **2.1%**, achieved **3.6%**; Bhakra-Nangal, Hirakud and Damodar Valley projects; **Community Development Programme (1952)**; IIT Kharagpur |
| **Second (1956-61)** | **Mahalanobis** model (P.C. Mahalanobis); thrust on **basic and capital-goods** industries (import substitution); target 4.5%; **Bhilai (USSR / Soviet Union), Rourkela (West Germany), Durgapur (United Kingdom)** steel plants; Industrial Policy Resolution **1956**; faced **foreign exchange** shortages and **inflation** |
| **Third (1961-66)** | Aimed at **self-reliance** and self-sufficiency in food; target **5.6%**; failed — **1962** China war, **1965** Pakistan war, 1965-66 drought |
| **Plan Holiday (1966-69)** | Three **annual plans**; groundwork of the **Green Revolution** |
| **Fourth (1969-74)** | "**Growth with stability** and progressive achievement of **self-reliance**"; aimed at correcting concentration of wealth and economic power (14 banks nationalised, **1969**); **Gadgil formula (1969)** for sharing central plan assistance among states |
| **Fifth (1974-78)** | "**Garibi Hatao**" (removal of poverty) and self-reliance; **Minimum Needs Programme**; ended a year early (1978) |
| **Rolling Plan (1978-80)** | Janata government; concept credited to **Gunnar Myrdal**; plan revised every year |
| **Sixth (1980-85)** | Poverty removal and employment; **IRDP** and **NREP** (1980); target 5.2% exceeded |
| **Seventh (1985-90)** | "**Food, Work and Productivity**"; target 5.0%, achieved ~6.0%; **Jawahar Rozgar Yojana (1989)** |
| **Annual Plans (1990-92)** | Political instability and the **1991** balance-of-payments crisis |
| **Eighth (1992-97)** | First plan after **LPG** reforms; target **5.6%**, achieved **6.8%**; human resource development |
| **Ninth (1997-2002)** | "**Growth with Social Justice and Equality**"; target 6.5%, achieved 5.4% |
| **Tenth (2002-07)** | **8%** growth target; aim of doubling per capita income in ten years; monitorable targets |
| **Eleventh (2007-12)** | "**Towards Faster and More Inclusive Growth**"; **9%** target; MGNREGA rolled out |
| **Twelfth (2012-17)** | "**Faster, More Inclusive and Sustainable Growth**"; **8%** target; the **last** Five-Year Plan |

## UPSC 2019 statement test

- From the **Second Plan** there was a determined thrust towards **substitution of basic and capital-goods industries** — **true**.
- The **Fourth Plan** adopted the objective of **correcting the earlier trend of increased concentration of wealth** and economic power — **true**.
- The **Fifth Plan** was the **first** to include the financial sector as an integral part of the plan — **false**.

## Don't confuse

- **Gadgil formula (1969)** is about **dividing central assistance among states** from the Fourth Plan; "Gadgil Yojana" for the Third Plan is a coaching label.
- **Sixth Plan (1980-85)** of the Congress government replaced the Janata **Rolling Plan**.
- Source books give slightly different "achieved" growth figures for several plans (e.g. Third 2.4% or 2.8%; Tenth 7.3% or 7.6%) — **targets** are the safer exam anchor.

**TL;DR**
- First: Harrod-Domar, 2.1% target, 3.6% achieved, Community Development 1952.
- Second: Mahalanobis, basic/capital goods; Bhilai (USSR), Rourkela (West Germany), Durgapur (UK).
- Fourth: growth with stability; Gadgil formula 1969. Fifth: Garibi Hatao, MNP.
- Rolling Plan: Gunnar Myrdal concept, 1978-80. Seventh: Food, Work and Productivity.
- Eighth: post-LPG, 6.8%. Ninth: growth with social justice and equality. Twelfth: last plan, 8% target.
keyPoints: First Plan: about 44.6% of outlay to agriculture; target 2.1%, achieved 3.6%; Community Development Programme 1952.
Second Plan steel plants: Bhilai (USSR), Rourkela (West Germany), Durgapur (UK).
UPSC 2019: Second Plan — thrust on substitution of basic and capital-goods industries; Fourth Plan — correcting concentration of wealth and economic power.
Fourth Plan objective: growth with stability and progressive achievement of self-reliance; Gadgil formula (1969).
Rolling Plan (1978-80) concept is credited to Gunnar Myrdal.
Sixth Plan launched IRDP and NREP (1980); Seventh Plan slogan: Food, Work and Productivity.
Ninth Plan theme: Growth with Social Justice and Equality; Eleventh: Towards Faster and More Inclusive Growth (9% target).
Twelfth Plan (2012-17): Faster, More Inclusive and Sustainable Growth; 8% target; last Five-Year Plan.

items.title: Planning Institutions — Dates, Office-Holders & NITI Aayog Machinery
items.body:
**In one line:** the Planning Commission (15 March 1950) and the NDC (6 August 1952) ran the plan era; NITI Aayog (1 January 2015) is a think-tank with a Governing Council, Regional Councils, a Vice-Chairperson and a CEO.

**Why it is asked:** dates, "first/last" office-holders and "which of these is a NITI body" are staple MCQs.

## Planning Commission and NDC

**The story**

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| Planning Commission set up | **15 March 1950** by a Cabinet (executive) resolution — **non-constitutional, non-statutory** (unlike the Finance Commission under **Article 280**) |
| Chairman | **Prime Minister** (first: **Jawaharlal Nehru**) |
| First Deputy Chairman | **Gulzarilal Nanda** |
| Last Deputy Chairman | **Montek Singh Ahluwalia** (2009-14) |
| National Development Council | Set up **6 August 1952**; PM-chaired; all CMs; **approved** the Five-Year Plans |

## NITI Aayog

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| Full form | **National Institution for Transforming India** |
| Created | **1 January 2015** by a **Union Cabinet resolution** (not by an Act or the Constitution) |
| Chairperson | **Prime Minister** |
| Governing Council | CMs of all states and UTs with legislatures, and Lt. Governors of other UTs; first meeting **8 February 2015** |
| Regional Councils | CMs and LGs of a region, for issues affecting more than one state |
| Vice-Chairperson | Appointed by the PM — first **Arvind Panagariya**; now (2026) **Ashok Lahiri** |
| CEO | Rank of Secretary to the Government of India — first **Sindhushree Khullar**; now (2026) **Anurag Jain** |
| Members | Full-time members, two part-time members, up to **four ex-officio** Union ministers, special invitees |
| Attached office | **DMEO** (Development Monitoring and Evaluation Office) |

## Hubs, indices and programmes of NITI Aayog

| Initiative | Year | Point |
|---|---|---|
| **Atal Innovation Mission (AIM)** | 2016 | **Atal Tinkering Labs** in schools; incubators |
| **Aspirational Districts Programme** | **January 2018** | **112** most backward districts; AP's are **Vizianagaram, Visakhapatnam, YSR Kadapa** (districts such as **Krishna** are not on the list) |
| **Champions of Change portal** | April 2018 | Built with the **Government of Andhra Pradesh** to rank aspirational districts (delta ranking) |
| **SDG India Index** | 2018 | State-wise SDG scores |
| **Composite Water Management Index** | 2018 | Water management by states |
| **India Innovation Index** | 2019 | Innovation ranking of states |
| **National Multidimensional Poverty Index** | 2021 | First national MPI (NFHS-4 baseline) |
| **Aspirational Blocks Programme** | **7 January 2023** | **500** blocks across 329 districts |

## Why the Planning Commission went — and what planning achieved

- **States** complained that the Commission was a top-down **control body** that ignored **local** needs and state-specific requirements.
- Planning was criticised for **bureaucratic** inefficiency, **over-centralisation** and a limited private-sector role.
- NITI Aayog was therefore set up as a policy **think-tank** and advisor with real-time monitoring, not a fund-allocating body.
- **Achievements** of planning: the Green Revolution, an industrial base of **steel** plants and PSUs, and social development.
- NITI's energy vision cites **450 GW** of renewable capacity by 2030.

## Federalism

- **Cooperative federalism** — Centre and states work together as equals (Governing Council).
- **Competitive federalism** — states compete on NITI's rankings and indices (SDG India Index, health and water indices).

## Andhra Pradesh angle

- **Swarna Andhra @2047** vision (launched **November 2024**) sets AP's goal for 2047 on **10 guiding principles ("Padi Sutralu")**, mirroring the national **Viksit Bharat @2047** goal.

**TL;DR**
- Planning Commission: 15 March 1950; first Deputy Chairman Gulzarilal Nanda; last Montek Singh Ahluwalia. NDC: 6 August 1952.
- NITI Aayog: 1 Jan 2015 by Cabinet resolution; first VC Arvind Panagariya, first CEO Sindhushree Khullar; now VC Ashok Lahiri, CEO Anurag Jain.
- Governing Council first met 8 Feb 2015; Regional Councils; DMEO attached office.
- AIM 2016; Aspirational Districts Jan 2018 (112; AP: Vizianagaram, Visakhapatnam, YSR Kadapa); Aspirational Blocks 7 Jan 2023 (500).
- Swarna Andhra @2047 (Nov 2024, 10 Padi Sutralu).
keyPoints: Planning Commission set up on 15 March 1950; first Deputy Chairman Gulzarilal Nanda; last Deputy Chairman Montek Singh Ahluwalia.
National Development Council set up on 6 August 1952.
NITI Aayog = National Institution for Transforming India; first Vice-Chairperson Arvind Panagariya, first CEO Sindhushree Khullar.
NITI Aayog Governing Council first met on 8 February 2015; Regional Councils handle multi-state issues.
DMEO (Development Monitoring and Evaluation Office) is attached to NITI Aayog.
Aspirational Districts Programme (January 2018): 112 districts; AP — Vizianagaram, Visakhapatnam, YSR Kadapa.
Champions of Change portal (April 2018) was built with the Government of Andhra Pradesh.
Aspirational Blocks Programme launched 7 January 2023 for 500 blocks.
Atal Innovation Mission (2016) runs Atal Tinkering Labs.
Swarna Andhra @2047 vision (Nov 2024) rests on 10 guiding principles (Padi Sutralu).

items.title: For Mains — Economic Planning & NITI Aayog
items.body:
A recurring **Paper-IV (Economy & Development)** theme — also usable in Paper-III governance questions — is whether India's move from directive planning to NITI Aayog's advisory model has served development. Build the answer across these dimensions.

| Dimension | Content to deploy |
|---|---|
| **Rationale for change** | Planning Commission's top-down, fund-allocating model mismatched the post-1991 market economy |
| **What changed** | Think-tank, no fund allocation (now Finance Commission), cooperative & competitive federalism |
| **Instruments** | 3-Year Action Agenda, 7-Year Strategy, 15-Year Vision; replaced Five-Year Plans |
| **Achievements** | Aspirational Districts, SDG India Index, National MPI, Atal Innovation Mission; data-driven governance |
| **Criticism** | No statutory status, no funds → limited leverage; 'advisory not transformative'; weak on employment |
| **Way forward** | Fiscal empowerment of states, outcome budgeting, Viksit Bharat @2047 |

**Data points & authorities to quote:** Planning Commission (1950, executive resolution) → NITI Aayog (**1 Jan 2015**); VC **Ashok Lahiri**, CEO **Anurag Jain** (2026); **15th Finance Commission** (Singh) handles devolution (41% vertical share); Twelfth Plan (2012-17) was the last; NITI's **SDG India Index** and **National MPI** feed competitive federalism; **Viksit Bharat @2047** vision. Thinkers/models: **Mahalanobis** (planning architect), **Harrod-Domar**, debates on 'cooperative federalism'.

**AP angle:** As a bifurcated, resource-constrained state, Andhra Pradesh benefits from NITI's cooperative-federalism and Aspirational Districts framework but has pressed for the special fiscal support promised under the AP Reorganisation Act 2014; AP's own planning (vision documents, Swarnandhra/development corporations) mirrors the national shift from plans to outcome-based strategy.

**Use in answers:** (1) frame as 'control → collaboration, allocation → facilitation'; (2) use a **two-column Planning Commission vs NITI Aayog table** as the body's spine; (3) cite the fund-allocation shift to the Finance Commission as the sharpest institutional change; (4) conclude that cooperative federalism must be matched by real fiscal empowerment of states.
keyPoints: Frame: rationale → what changed → instruments → achievements → criticism → way forward.
Key institutional shift: fund allocation moved from Planning Commission to the Finance Commission; NITI is advisory.
Quote NITI (1 Jan 2015), VC Ashok Lahiri, CEO Anurag Jain (2026); Twelfth Plan (2012-17) last; Viksit Bharat @2047.
Criticism: no statutory/fund power limits leverage; advisory not transformative.
AP angle: cooperative federalism + Aspirational Districts vs demand for Reorganisation-Act fiscal support.
